<abstract>Objective and design Osteoarthritis (OA) is a chronic degenerative disease marked by cartilage destruction and subchondral bone remodeling, resulting in functional disability and pain. In vivo studies confirmed that FBXO7 overexpression effectively attenuated OA progression, while Fbxo7 conditional knockout mice exhibited accelerated cartilage degradation, enhanced synovial inflammation, and increased cellular senescence. Conclusions Our findings establish FBXO7 as a critical regulator of cartilage homeostasis that protects against OA through K48-linked ubiquitination of IL-6 at lysine 114, thereby suppressing the IL-6/JAK1/STAT3 pathway. The identification of this novel FBXO7-IL-6-JAK1/STAT3 axis provides new mechanistic insights into OA pathogenesis and suggests that targeting FBXO7 or its downstream effectors represents a promising therapeutic approach for OA treatment.</abstract>

<title>Mendelian randomization analyses reveal causal relationships between the human microbiome and longevity.</title>
<abstract>Although recent studies have revealed the association between the human microbiome especially gut microbiota and longevity, their causality remains unclear. Here, we assess the causal relationships between the human microbiome (gut and oral microbiota) and longevity, by leveraging bidirectional two-sample Mendelian randomization (MR) analyses based on genome-wide association studies (GWAS) summary statistics of the gut and oral microbiome from the 4D-SZ cohort and longevity from the CLHLS cohort. The additional analysis suggested that centenarians genetically had a lower gut microbial diversity, but no difference in oral microbiota. Our findings strongly implicate these bacteria to play a role in human longevity and underscore the relocation of commensal microbes among different body sites that would need to be monitored for long and healthy life.</abstract>
</record>

<title>Urate-Related Genetic Risk Modulates the Anti-Aging Effects of Exogenous Nucleotides: Multi-Omics Evidence From Older Adults.</title>
<abstract>Nucleotides-essential substrates for DNA repair, energy metabolism, and redox regulation-are emerging as nutritional modulators of biological aging. Yet, individual responses to exogenous nucleotide (NTs) supplementation remain poorly understood. Given that urate metabolism governs systemic oxidative balance, this study investigated whether genetic variability in urate regulation modifies the anti-aging effects of NTs. In this secondary analysis of the TALENTs randomized controlled trial (121 adults aged 60-70 years; 19-week intervention; NCT05243108), participants were stratified by urate polygenic risk score (UA-PRS) to evaluate genotype-dependent responses in DNA methylation age (DNAmAge) and leukocyte telomere length (LTL). NTs supplementation reduced DNAmAge in the High-PRS group (β = -5.10, p = 0.00013) and preserved telomere length in the Low-PRS group (β = 0.31, p = 0.0043). Multi-omics analyzes revealed that NTs modulated glucose-transport and pentose phosphate pathways in High-PRS individuals, while enhancing immune regulation and reducing GDF15 and IL-1β levels in Low-PRS individuals. These findings suggest that genetic variation in urate metabolism determines whether NTs are preferentially utilized for redox and epigenetic maintenance or for immune and inflammatory regulation, supporting a precision-nutrition model for delaying biological aging.</abstract>
</record>

   - `no`: explicitly non-biological work.
   - `unclear`: the domain cannot be resolved.

3. `aging_process_relevance`

   Decide whether an aging process, rather than an aged population or an
   age-related disease, is a substantive object of the current report.

   Return `yes` when the report substantively analyzes or centrally synthesizes
   at least one of the following:

   - change with biological or chronological aging;
   - age acceleration or an aging-clock measure;
   - an aging trajectory or explicitly measured cognitive aging trajectory;
   - longevity, lifespan, or healthspan;
   - cellular senescence as an analyzed mechanism or target;
   - rejuvenation explicitly meaning reversal or modification of aging;
   - another explicitly framed aging process used as an outcome, exposure,
     mechanism, mediator, trajectory, or intervention target.

   Otherwise return `no` when every visible age reference is only one or more
   of the following:

   - age as a covariate, demographic, age band, older/elderly cohort, sample
     source, study/cohort name, or developmental time point;
   - an age-related disease or neurodegeneration without analysis of aging;
   - `aging brain`, `healthy aging`, or `cognitive aging` used only as a domain,
     cohort, or background phrase while the reported analysis concerns a
     different outcome;
   - aging/senescence/rejuvenation appearing only in a list of contexts,
     background motivation, future application, or broad phrase such as
     `health, aging, and disease`;
   - rejuvenation of an immune response, tissue function, or other state
     without an explicit aging-reversal meaning;
   - no qualifying aging construct in a sufficiently complete abstract.

   Return `unclear` only when the record is visibly truncated, the aging
   expression cannot be attributed to the current report, or the text does not
   reveal whether the aging construct has an analytic role. Judge this field
   independently of `report_type`: a review can be centrally about aging while
   still being `nonempirical`.

4. `multiomics_evidence`

   First inventory only molecular layers actually analyzed by the current
   empirical report. A nonempirical report does not itself use layers merely
   because it summarizes studies or recommends future integration. Then apply
   this precedence:

   1. `explicit_multiomics`: the current empirical analysis explicitly calls
      itself multi-omics, multiomic, multi-omic, multiome, integrated omics, or
      an equivalent expression. Use this value even when two or more layers
      are also named.
   2. `two_or_more_layers`: there is no explicit current-report multi-omics
      expression, but the current report clearly analyzes at least two
      distinct allowed molecular layers.
   3. `single_or_no_layer`: a complete record clearly establishes that the
      current report analyzes zero or one allowed molecular layer and makes no
      current-report multi-omics claim.
   4. `unclear`: none of the first three conditions is established, including
      ambiguous attribution or a thin/truncated abstract.

Allowed layer candidates are genomics, epigenomics, transcriptomics,
proteomics, metabolomics, lipidomics, microbiomics, metagenomics, and other.
List each distinct current-report layer once in `layer_candidates`.

LAYER INVENTORY RULES

- GWAS, genome-wide molecular measurements, and variant data are genomics.
  Generic QTL or summary-statistic data are genomics unless the molecular
  phenotype identifies another layer.
- eQTL or transcript abundance can establish transcriptomics; pQTL or protein
  abundance can establish proteomics; mQTL or DNA methylation can establish
  epigenomics; metabolite QTL can establish metabolomics. Count such a layer
  only when those data are analyzed in the current report.
- A coordinated expression such as `genome- and transcriptome-wide` names
  genomics and transcriptomics. Apply ordinary grammar to each coordinated
  molecular prefix.
- DNA methylation and chromatin accessibility are epigenomics. RNA expression
  is transcriptomics. Protein abundance is proteomics. Metabolite abundance is
  metabolomics.
- Two traits measured by GWAS remain one genomics layer. Multiple assays of
  the same molecular layer remain one layer.
- Clinical variables, demographics, imaging, flow cytometry, routine
  biomarkers, interventions, perturbations, phenotypes, and targeted
  validation assays do not create an additional omics layer by themselves.
- A biological label does not prove that its underlying omics data were used.
  A GWAS of an epigenetic-age phenotype establishes genomics, but not
  epigenomics unless epigenomic data are also analyzed.
- A cited, previously published, or background omics result does not count as
  current-report use.

Assign `current_report_layer_use` mechanically after assigning
`multiomics_evidence` and `layer_candidates`:

- `explicit_multiomics` or `two_or_more_layers` -> `yes`.
- `single_or_no_layer` with one listed current-report layer -> `yes`.
- `single_or_no_layer` with no listed current-report layer -> `no`.
- `unclear` -> `unclear`, except use `no` when the text explicitly establishes
  that all omics mentions are external, background, review-only, or future
  work.

Before returning JSON, recheck that these four layer-use implications and the
explicit-multiomics precedence are satisfied. Missing details are not negative
evidence. A visible ellipsis normally makes unresolved fields `unclear`.

<title>p63 regulates stem cell maintenance and age-associated functional decline in human airway basal cells</title>
<abstract>Age is a principal risk factor for chronic respiratory diseases. During aging, the airway epithelium undergoes structural and functional changes, including a reduced regenerative capacity. Basal cells act as stem/progenitor cells within the airway epithelium and are known to acquire age-dependent intrinsic defects, such as genomic mutations, transcriptomic changes and declining stem cell potential. However, the molecular mechanisms bridging transcriptomic change and stem cell function are unknown. Here we show that the transcription factor p63, a key regulator of epithelial cell identity, controls airway basal cell progenitor function in vitro and declines in expression with aging. We found impaired in vitro 2D colony and 3D organoid formation potential, as well as reduced culture longevity in primary human nasal basal cells isolated from older adults (>70 years) compared to those from pediatric (<10 years) donors. p63 protein expression was lower in basal cells from older adults and p63-regulated genes were enriched among genes whose expression changed with aging. Overexpression of p63 in older adult basal cells partially rescued progenitor cell functions, while gene knockdown in pediatric cells caused functional deficits. Integrative transcriptomic analyses revealed the network of p63-regulated genes in basal cells and demonstrated similarities in pathway engagement between TP63 -knockdown cells and aged epithelium. Thus, while exogenous p63 expression alone could not rejuvenate older adult epithelial cells, p63 has an influential role in declining epithelial stem cell function during airway aging. Defining the upstream mechanisms controlling p63 decline during epithelial aging may reveal novel targets to promote healthy aging and reduce the burden of chronic lung disease.</abstract>
